title: Google Brings Agentic AI to Gemini for Enterprise: Key Features and Business Impact
excerpt: Google announced a unified agentic AI for Gemini Enterprise, enabling autonomous multi-system task execution, co-worker identity, and custom tooling.
metaDescription: Google launched agentic AI in Gemini Enterprise, giving the AI its own Workspace identity and third-party model support. Here is what teams need to know.
content:
Google is pushing Gemini past the chat window. At a recent Google Cloud event covered by TechCrunch, the company showed off an agentic setup designed to run tasks across company software instead of just answering prompts. Following releases like [Google's Gemini 4 Argon: What You Need to Know About the New Frontier AI Model](/blog/googles-gemini-4-argon-frontier-ai-model-released), this is a clear shift toward letting an AI handle operational workloads directly.

## What was announced

Google is shipping an enterprise agent built directly into Gemini that plans, executes, and audits work across corporate tools. Sundar Pichai announced that Gemini has passed 1 billion monthly active users, and nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies already run Gemini Enterprise. Because of that existing base, Google is rolling this out to corporate customers first. They want to work through latency, security, and scale before bringing it to consumer accounts.

Here are the specific platform details from the event:

* **A dedicated corporate identity:** The agent gets an actual Google Workspace account with its own email address, internal permissions, and directory profile.
* **Cross-tool integration:** It connects directly with Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, and Snowflake.
* **MCP server support:** Works with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so you can hook it into internal APIs and external tools through standard interfaces.
* **Unified tasks inbox:** A dashboard where you can see Gemini's step-by-step reasoning, executed code, loaded tools, and subagents.
* **Cost controls:** Admins can configure smart model routing and set hard, real-time spending caps to prevent runaway inference bills.
* **Multi-model selection:** Gemini picks the default model, but you can swap it out. Google is even offering third-party models here, starting with Anthropic's Claude.

## What's new in Gemini's agentic shift

Most AI tools wait for a prompt, return text, and stop. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian explained that this architecture focuses on "objectives, not just instructions." You give the agent an end goal. It breaks the project into stages, triggers subagents, calls internal tools, and works through each step on its own.

That changes how software teams can use these tools:

1. **Autonomous execution:** The agent handles multi-step jobs without someone holding its hand. It can write code, book travel, set up meetings, or trigger build pipelines across systems.
2. **True co-worker workflow:** It functions like another teammate on your roster. You can assign it a Jira ticket, forward it an email, tag it in Slack, or mention it inside Google Workspace and ServiceNow.
3. **Dedicated audit trails:** When the agent commits code to Git or runs queries against Postgres, those actions get logged under the agent's identity. It doesn't impersonate a human engineer or hide behind someone else's token.
4. **Third-party models on Google Cloud:** Google isn't locking you into Gemini weights. You can route specific steps through Anthropic's Claude, and they plan to support private and open-source models later.

## What it means for businesses and developers

For engineering teams—including our crew here in Patna building backend services and distributed apps—this changes how we link AI to production environments. If you maintain pipelines that already require steps like [hardening webhook security: mitigating replay and forgery attacks](/blog/hardening-webhook-security-mitigating-replay-forgery-attacks), you know the headache of granting write access to external scripts. An agent with an auditable identity and MCP support makes that integration much cleaner.

Here is how teams can put this to work:

* **DevOps and delivery:** You assign a backlog task in GitHub or Jira directly to the agent. It reviews requirements in Confluence, inspects the repo, writes code, runs test suites, and opens a pull request under its own name.
* **Cross-system workflows:** An engineer can ask the agent to query a Databricks or Snowflake cluster, draft an analysis, push a summary to Slack, and drop a review meeting onto the calendar. One objective handles all four tools.
* **Vendor flexibility:** You aren't stuck with Google models if a specific task demands Claude's style or logic. Switching between models based on price and performance happens right in the console.
* **Budget protection:** Autonomous agent loops can burn tokens fast if they get stuck. Real-time spend caps keep you from waking up to an unexpected cloud invoice.

Early testers include On, Shopify, and PayPal, alongside current Gemini Enterprise clients like BNP Paribas, Merck, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.

## How to try it or prepare

Google is releasing this to Gemini Enterprise accounts first, with interfaces spanning desktop (Windows, macOS), mobile, command-line tools, Slack, ServiceNow, and Microsoft 365.

If you want your systems ready when access opens, take these steps:

* **Audit directory permissions:** The agent gets its own user identity. Review your Google Workspace and access lists now so it only touches the repositories, documents, and calendars you approve under zero-trust rules.
* **Map your data sources:** List the databases (Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake) and project management boards (Jira, Confluence) the agent will need read or write access to.
* **Build standard MCP servers:** If your team uses proprietary internal services, wrap them in Model Context Protocol servers so the agent can discover and execute those endpoints cleanly.
* **Set spending and routing rules:** Decide ahead of time which jobs stay on Gemini, when to route work to Claude, and where to place hard daily budget limits in Google Cloud.

## The takeaway

Google's update turns Gemini from an assistant you chat with into an authenticated worker that runs operations across your tools. By giving the agent a distinct corporate identity, adding native MCP support, and allowing external models like Claude, Google Cloud is setting a practical pattern for how development teams delegate real work to software agents.
